Amazon $AMZN shares down almost 6% after-hours as earnings miss and capex soars accelerating its cash flow burn.

That was despite AWS growing 39.3% to $46.0B, its fastest in nearly five years and above the $45.29B consensus (TipRanks), although short of the ~42% buyside whisper (ZeroHedge). Jassy now projects 40%+ AWS growth in both 2027 and 2028.  

But:
▪️ Net capex of $75.9B vs. $42.4B of operating cash flow = a $33.5B cash burn in one quarter. Bloomberg consensus was a $7.7B outflow (per ZeroHedge) 
▪️ Trailing 12-month free cash flow: −$42.4B, from −$7.6B in Q2 
▪️ $48.1B of new long-term debt in Q3; long-term debt now $173.1B vs. $65.6B at the end of 2025 
▪️ Interest expense more than tripled to $1.7B and now exceeds Amazon's $1.2B of interest income 
▪️ Holding the $220B 2026 capex plan implies ~$47.8B in Q4, 37% below Q3. Either spending slows sharply, or the $220B estimate gets blown through  

Weak spots under the beat: 
▪️ AWS added $3.75B of revenue from Q2, vs. $4.65B the quarter before (despite an extra day), and its margin slipped to 38.7% from 39.4% 
▪️AWS lagged its peers: Azure +48%, Google Cloud +103% (including TPU sales). Google Cloud added ~$15.5B of revenue year over year, more than AWS's $13.0B, from a base less than half the size.
▪️ Ads +12% ex-currency, $19.64B vs. $20.82B est. Amazon blames Prime Day timing, but Q2 and Q3 combined grew 18.1% vs. 23.2% over the same stretch last year 
▪️ The record 13.9% operating margin is mix: every segment's margin fell from Q2 
▪️ Operating income +61% year over year is actually +29% vs. last year's figure excluding the FTC and severance charges  

Q3 Revenue $201.9B vs. $202.31B est.; EPS $1.89 vs. $1.96 (TipRanks). 

Q4 guide: sales $240B to $247B (FactSet consensus $244.17B); operating income $28.5B to $33.5B, a $31B midpoint vs. ~$33B Street.

Intel ($INTC) shares down around 16% after-hours despite a Q3 beat as current quarter guidance came in well below expectations.  

Q3 vs. TipRanks consensus:
▪️ Adj. EPS 52c vs. 41c expected
▪️ Revenue $16.51B (+21%) vs. $16.56B 
▪️ Non-GAAP gross margin 44.1%, vs. 42.0%

Q4 guidance vs consensus
▪️ Revenue $15B–$16B vs. $17.06B. Midpoint 9% below, −6% q/q 
▪️ Adj. EPS 25c vs. 44c 
▪️ Gross margin guided to 38.0%, down 6.1 pts from Q3   

Data represented all the growth: 
▪️ Data Center & AI +78% to $7.3B (fastest in 15 years), vs. $6.7B expected per MarketWatch 
▪️ It supplied 112% of Intel's $2.86B revenue gain. Ex-data center, sales FELL 3.6% 
▪️ Segment op margin 41.5% vs. 23.4% a year ago ▪️ PC chips −5% to $8.1B vs. $8.9B expected, −9% q/q  

Intel blames memory-driven PC weakness it says will last through at least 1H 2027 and an Israel fab disruption (explosion, per MarketWatch). 

It sees the PC market −10% in 2027 after −12% in 2026 (Bloomberg).  

Inventory rose 4.6% q/q to $13.1B into a PC downturn.  

So the AI CPU demand is real, and data center is now Intel's profit engine. But a stock up 140%+ this year (FT) was priced for a smoother transition, and a guide that cuts revenue, margin and EPS at once isn't one.

Domestic buyers again were forced to try pick up the slack from softer foreign demand in today’s $44 billion 7-year Treasury auction. 

At Monday’s 2-year, indirect bidders (which include foreign buyers) fell to the lowest since November 2021, and Tuesday’s 5-year was still below average. Today was a similar story, but direct (domestic) bidders took the second-largest share on record. That kept the result right in line with expectations and left dealers with less than at either of the previous two auctions:

▪️ Tail: 0.0bps (on the screws), much better than the +0.7bps in September (the biggest since March) and the +0.2bps six-month average. Interestingly, it was the 4th 7-year on the screws in 2026
▪️ Bid/cover: 2.46, up from 2.42 but below the 2.49 six-month average
▪️ Dealers: 9.4%, the least since December 2025, vs 12.5% in September and the 12.1% six-month average (13.0% at the 2-year and 10.6% at the 5-year)
▪️ Indirect (incl. foreign): 57.8%, up slightly from 57.2% (the lowest since November 2025) but well below the 63.7% six-month average
▪️ Direct (domestic): 32.8%, the highest since July 2025 and second-highest on record (after July 2025’s 33.7%), vs the 24.2% six-month average
▪️ High yield: 4.894%, down from September’s record 5.085%

At all three auctions this week, indirect bidders took a below-average share (45.7%, 60.0% and 57.8%), offset at least in part by direct bidders taking more (41.3%, 29.4% and 32.8%). @investingLive’s Greg Michalowski gave it a B-.

After months of speculation that she would leave before her eight-year term ends in October 2027, European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde announced today that she will step down on February 7, 2027, just hours ahead of the Governing Council’s latest rate decision, according to Bloomberg. Hers is the third of the six Executive Board seats set to turn over by May.

Lagarde becomes only the second president in the ECB’s 28-year history to leave early, after Wim Duisenberg, whose shortened stint had been agreed in advance to break a France-Germany deadlock before the bank’s launch.

Lagarde, 70, told fellow policymakers she wanted “greater freedom to express her views” because she could not stay neutral on developments in France ahead of its April presidential election, the Financial Times reported. She has ruled out running herself and has been in talks to chair the World Economic Forum. In a video message, she said she leaves with “a sense of good work done, and an ECB that is fit for the future,” per Bloomberg.

Three of the six Executive Board seats — the presidency, the chief economist and the markets portfolio — turn over by May. Isabel Schnabel is leaving a year early to join the International Monetary Fund and Philip Lane’s term expires in May, so governments will likely try to settle all three in one deal, with EU summits in November and December, per Bloomberg.

For the presidency, Spain is backing Pablo Hernández de Cos, general manager of the Bank for International Settlements and former Bank of Spain governor, while the Dutch government is backing former Dutch central bank chief Klaas Knot, the FT reported. Economists surveyed by Bloomberg in October see De Cos as the favorite. Knot built a reputation as a hawk during the eurozone debt crisis but has since softened into a pragmatist seen as responsive to bond-market stress, according to The Wall Street Journal, which also noted that an outsider can’t be ruled out given Lagarde herself was a last-minute pick in a 2019 package deal.

The timing also lets President Emmanuel Macron help pick Lagarde’s successor before his final term ends, with far-right candidate Marine Le Pen leading French polls, which risks accusations of political encroachment on the ECB’s independence, Bloomberg added. Banque de France’s governor also left early, with Macron naming his chief of staff, Emmanuel Moulin, to the post.

The news barely moved markets following the announcement. The euro was down 0.1% against the dollar at $1.114, per the FT, while the 10-year German Bund yield was 1 basis point lower at 3.36% and the French-German 10-year spread held at 154 basis points, according to Bloomberg. That spread recently hit its widest since 2011, and French long-term borrowing costs topped 5% last week for the first time since 2002 per the FT. Berenberg chief economist Holger Schmieding told the FT the departure doesn’t change the outlook for ECB policy or for how the bank handles French risks.

Morgan Stanley's US economists see a Q3 strong advance print this morning, tracking 3.1%, but say "the main story" is consumption, which they have growing 3.7% along with business investment. Trade and inventories are expected to be offsetting outliers in either direction.

Their Q3 build, contributions to growth in percentage points (Q2 in parentheses): 
▪️ Consumer spending +2.5 (+2.5) 
▪️ Business investment +1.5 (+1.3), growing 10.2% with equipment up 15% 
▪️ Inventories +1.7 (−0.5) 
▪️ Government +0.3 (0.0) 
▪️ Residential −0.2 (+0.1) 
▪️ Net exports −2.9 (−1.1), as imports "offset part of the contribution from AI capital spending"  

The caveat: MS says some of the consumer strength "may be more statistical than real." Leftover seasonal patterns push inflation higher in the first quarter, which depresses real spending early in the year and flatters it later.  Their 3.7% Q3 after 3.8% in Q2 still works out to only 2.6% year over year, "solid, but not exceptionally strong."

Atlanta Fed GDPNow’s final Q3 nowcast came in at 3.27% Wednesday, the least since it initiated tracking for the quarter and down from its 6.18% peak on August 3. Q3 GDP is out later this morning.

How much weight to put on it? Over the past two years its last reading before GDP has been either very close or well off, with little in between:

▪ Within a tenth in 4 of the last 8 quarters (Q3 & Q4 ‘24, Q2 ‘25, Q2 ‘26)
▪ Off 0.75 pt or more in the other 4, two of them (Q4 ‘25 & Q1 ‘26) mostly from the federal shutdown
▪ Since 2014 (ex-2020), its average miss is 0.59 pt: within half a point half the time, within a point 84% of the time

Two tendencies worth noting for today:
▪ When GDPNow falls more than half a point in the final month (it’s down 1.75 pts from 5.02% on Sept 25), the actual print has come in above its final reading in 16 of 22 quarters
▪ In third quarters specifically, the print has come in above GDPNow’s final reading in 10 of 14 quarters (ex-2020), by an average of 0.31 pt

This quarter it has company: as of Friday, six of the seven major GDP trackers I follow were between 3.1% and 3.7%, with the NY Fed the outlier at 2.67%. All seven are well above the Blue Chip consensus of ~2.5%.
